messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Viktor

Viktor was seventy-six when he walked into the clinic on a Tuesday morning in November, moving with the careful deliberation of a man who no longer fully trusted his own legs. He had spent forty-three years managing hotels—the Grandview in downtown Denver, the Riverside in Aspen, most recently a boutique property near Boulder—and had built a reputation for precision and unflappable composure. That composure had fractured on a March afternoon two years ago when a contractor's crew had ruptured a chemical line in the basement mechanical room while Viktor was conducting his routine inspection. The acrid smell hit him first—a choking, metallic burn that coated the back of his throat—followed by the sound of liquid hissing across concrete. He had stumbled backward, his lungs seizing, vision swimming, and in those moments before he reached the stairs, he had been certain he was dying. The hospital confirmed chemical pneumonitis, a course of steroids, and a prognosis of full recovery. But recovery, Viktor had come to understand, was not the same as healing.

The first months had been manageable. He returned to work in May, determined to reclaim his routine. But by July, something had shifted. Unexpected noises—a car backfiring, a door slamming, even the hiss of the espresso machine in the hotel lobby—would send his heart into a gallop, his palms slick with sweat. He had come to believe that his body was no longer his to command, that it had become an adversary, erupting in panic at moments when his rational mind insisted there was no danger. The knowledge that he could not control these reactions, that his own physiology had turned traitor, had settled into a deep, immobilizing dread. This persistent sense of threat—that his body might betray him again without warning, that danger could arrive unannounced—quietly confirmed the conviction that had taken root: the world was fundamentally unsafe, and he was powerless to protect himself. On nights when the threat felt highest, when his body seemed most poised to betray him, the memory was hardest to keep at bay—it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome, pulled out of him by the adrenaline, fully formed, as though his vigilance had summoned it. He was certain now that he could not stop bad things from happening—that the world was fundamentally unsafe and his body would betray him again without warning. This conviction seeped into every room of his apartment. Having decided that the world was fundamentally unsafe and his body could not be trusted, Viktor walked through his apartment already braced for danger—the threat arrived with him before anything had happened, a shadow cast by his own certainty of vulnerability. Even at home, behind locked doors, he felt exposed, scanning for threats, his shoulders rigid, his breath shallow. He had begun to believe that safety existed in only a handful of places: his bedroom with the curtains drawn, his therapist's office, the car with the windows up. Everywhere else felt permeable, hostile.

The memories themselves were fragmented and strange. Sometimes Viktor would be standing in his kitchen, reaching for a coffee mug, when he would be flooded with the full emotional intensity of that March afternoon—the terror, the suffocation, the conviction that he was dying—but without any clear image, as though the fear had detached from its source and become free-floating. Other times, a particular smell would surface: not the chemical itself, but something close enough—cleaning solution, a stranger's cologne, even the mineral scent of the hotel's humidifier—and suddenly he could taste that acrid burn, could feel his lungs constricting, the memory arriving in pieces that never quite assembled into a coherent narrative. These fragmentary recollections had begun to feel intolerable, and Viktor had learned that if he kept the television on loud enough, if he filled every moment with noise and distraction, the memories could not find their footing—silence was the enemy, and so he had become dependent on constant sound to keep them at bay. These fragmentary recollections had begun to feel like proof that he was losing his mind. The fear that he was "going crazy" had become as present as the fear of the chemical itself, and Viktor had developed a habit of monitoring his own thoughts constantly, watching for signs of deterioration, checking whether his thinking was still rational. This vigilance exhausted him but felt necessary, a kind of mental sentry duty.

To manage the intrusions, Viktor had turned to distraction. He kept the television on almost constantly now, the volume loud enough to drown out any unexpected sound from the street or hallway. Music played in his car during the short drives he still permitted himself. The noise created a kind of buffer, a wall between himself and the unpredictable world, and as long as the sound continued, he could maintain a fragile sense of control. He had learned that if he kept the television loud enough, if he stayed in motion, the fragmentary recollections could not find their footing—but the moment the noise stopped, the memories were there again, waiting. But the distraction fed back into his sense of helplessness: he recognized that he needed the noise to feel safe, and that dependency itself became evidence that he was unraveling, that he could no longer manage his own mind. His work had suffered. He had taken medical leave in September, ostensibly temporary, but the thought of returning to the hotel—of being in that building, of hearing the mechanical systems hum, of navigating the basement where the exposure had occurred—was impossible. He had avoided the site entirely, unable even to drive past it. His colleagues had stopped calling. His ex-wife, with whom he had maintained cordial contact for years, had become distant after he cancelled three consecutive dinner invitations, unable to explain why he could not leave his apartment in the evening.

What had finally brought Viktor to seek help was a moment of clarity that felt more like capitulation. He was sitting in his darkened bedroom, the television murmuring, when he realized he could not remember the last time he had felt safe. Not just safe—present. The thought that he might spend the remainder of his life in this small, shrinking space, waiting for disaster, had broken something open. He arrived at the clinic asking a single question: whether there was any way to trust his body again, or whether he would have to learn to live as a prisoner of its betrayals. To stop the memories coming at night, Viktor started keeping the television on constantly, the noise a barrier between himself and the intrusions that seemed to arrive whenever silence gave them room to breathe.
